blocks.text: a) Identification of carbonate CO₃²⁻ radical

blocks.caption: Identification of carbonate radical
rows: Take about 2 g of solid carbonate sample in a clean test tube and then add about 5 cm³ of dilute HCl solution. Pass the gas evolved in the above step through a solution of lime water.
Effervescence takes place during which a gas evolves briskly, that turns lime water turns milky.

blocks.text: Reactions involved in the above steps

blocks.text_alt: Ca(OH)₂(aq) (lime water) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) (white ppt) + H₂O(l)

blocks.text: (b) Identification of chloride (Cl¹⁻), Bromide (Br¹⁻) and Iodide (I¹⁻) radicals

blocks.caption: Identification of chloride, bromide and iodide radicals
rows: Take 2 g of solid sample in a test tube and add 5 cm³ of distilled water to make the aqueous solution. Add a few drops of dil. HNO₃ solution to acidify the solution of the salt, finally add about 5 cm³ of aqueous AgNO₃.
A thick white precipitate is formed which dissolves in aq.NH₃.
Take 2 g of solid sample in a test tube and add 5 cm³ of distilled water to dissolve the salt. Add a few drops of dil. HNO₃ to acidify the above solution. Finally add 5 cm³ of aqueous AgNO₃.
A thick cream-yellow precipitate is formed.
Take 2 g of solid sample and dissolve it in 5 cm³ of distilled waler. Add a few drops of dil. HNO₃ to make it acidic. Finally add 5 cm³ aqueous AgNO₃.
A bright yellow precipitate is formed.

blocks.text: Reactions involved in the above tests

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: In the above tests for the detection of halide ions, dilute nitric acid is added to prevent the precipitation of carbonate ions along-with halide ions.

blocks.alt: Three test tubes labelled A, B and C. A contains a white precipitate tagged CHLORIDE (WHITE), B a cream precipitate tagged BROMIDE (CREAM) and C a yellow precipitate tagged IODIDE (YELLOW).
blocks.caption: Figure 16.7: Observation of reactions of halide ions with AgNO3 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.7).
Identification of nitrate radical
rows: Take 2 g of solid sample in a clean test tube and dissolve it in 5 cm³ distilled water. Add to it 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution. Finally add 3 g of powdered aluminium metal.
A characteristic smell of NH₃ gas is felt near the mouth of test tube. This gas turns red litmus paper blue.

blocks.text: Aluminium metal reduces nitrate ions to ammonium ions which then react with aqueous NaOH to evolve ammonia gas. The reduction of NO₃¹⁻ with aluminium metal is a redox reaction in which Al metal acts as a cathode and reduces nitrate ions to ammonia gas.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: There is no cathode in this test: no cell or electrolysis is involved. Aluminium acts as the reducing agent. It is oxidised (to [Al(OH)₄]¹⁻) and reduces nitrate ions to ammonia gas.

blocks.alt: A test tube of test solution held at an angle over a Bunsen burner, with a strip of litmus paper (red changing to blue) at its mouth. Tags: LITMUS PAPER, TEST SOLUTION, BUNSEN BURNER.
blocks.caption: Nitrate test (original drawing after the figure printed in the textbook).
Identification of sulphate radical
rows: Take 3 g of solid sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 5 cm³ of distilled water. Acidify the solution with a few drops of dil. HNO₃ and then add 5 cm³ barium nitrate solution.
A heavy white precipitate of BaSO₄ is formed.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Dilute nitric acid is added to destroy any carbonate ions present in the solution as an impurity.
